title: Frankenstein
author: Mary Shelley

sections.authorBiography: Mary Wollstonecraft Godwin was born in London on 30 August 1797, the daughter of two of the most famous radical writers of the 1790s: the philosopher William Godwin (author of Political Justice) and the feminist Mary Wollstonecraft (author of A Vindication of the Rights of Woman). Wollstonecraft died of puerperal fever about eleven days after the birth, so Mary grew up with her mother's books rather than her mother. In 1814, at sixteen, she left England with the married poet Percy Bysshe Shelley; they married in December 1816, weeks after his first wife's suicide. She began Frankenstein at eighteen and published it at twenty. Her adult life was marked by loss: three of her four children died young, and Percy drowned in Italy in July 1822. She supported herself and her surviving son by writing, produced novels including The Last Man (1826), edited Percy's poems, and died in London on 1 February 1851.
sections.historicalContext: The novel was born in the summer of 1816, the "year without a summer," when ash from the 1815 eruption of Mount Tambora in Indonesia chilled and darkened Europe. Mary, Percy, her stepsister Claire Clairmont, Lord Byron and Byron's physician John Polidori were kept indoors near Lake Geneva, and Byron proposed that each write a ghost story. The science in the air was electricity and life: Luigi Galvani had made dissected frogs' legs twitch with current, and in 1803 his nephew Giovanni Aldini publicly applied current to the corpse of an executed man in London. The book also belongs to Romanticism, a movement that prized feeling, nature and the solitary genius, and that was fascinated by Prometheus, the Titan who stole fire for humankind and was punished for it; the novel's subtitle is The Modern Prometheus. Behind it, too, is Mary's inheritance from her parents' arguments about education, injustice and how society makes people what they are.

publicationAndReception.publication: Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus appeared anonymously in three volumes on 1 January 1818 (London: Lackington, Hughes, Harding, Mavor and Jones), in an edition of about 500 copies, with a preface by Percy Shelley and a dedication to William Godwin. A second edition (1823), arranged by Godwin, named Mary as author after a stage version, Richard Brinsley Peake's Presumption, became a hit. In 1831 she revised the text heavily for Colburn and Bentley's Standard Novels and added the Introduction that tells the story of its origin; that 1831 text is the one we read.
publicationAndReception.then: Early reviews were split. Walter Scott, in Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine (March 1818), praised its "original genius" and assumed Percy Shelley was the author; John Wilson Croker in the Quarterly Review called it "a tissue of horrible and disgusting absurdity." Many reviewers were uneasy with a story that seemed to question God and moral order, and with an anonymous author linked to Godwin's radicals.
publicationAndReception.now: Today Frankenstein is one of the most taught novels in English. Brian Aldiss (Billion Year Spree, 1973) called it the origin of science fiction; feminist critics beginning with Ellen Moers (Literary Women, 1976) read it as a "birth myth" shaped by Mary's experience of pregnancy and infant death; others read it through politics, race, disability and bioethics. Its title has become shorthand in debates about genetic engineering and artificial intelligence, and 2018 brought bicentenary editions and projects worldwide.

sections.overview: A ship's captain, Robert Walton, sailing toward the North Pole, writes letters to his sister. In the ice he rescues a dying stranger, Victor Frankenstein, who tells him how, as a young student, he discovered the secret of life and built a living being. What happens to Victor, his family and his creation is told in three nested voices: Walton's, Victor's and, at the center, the creature's own. The book asks what we owe the things we make and the people we reject.

mainThemes.note: what a maker owes what it makes; watch how often the creature asks to be cared for and how Victor answers.
the hunger to discover, shared by Walton and Victor; ask whether the book condemns curiosity or something more specific.
almost every character is cut off from someone; notice who is allowed to belong and why.
is anyone born a monster, or are monsters made by how they are treated?
mountains, ice and storms that awe and dwarf human beings.

sections.whyItMatters: Frankenstein is the founding story for every argument about technology that outruns responsibility, from gene editing to artificial intelligence, and its creature still speaks for anyone judged by appearance before being heard. It also shows students that a teenager wrote one of the most influential books in the world.

spoilerOverview.text: Victor abandons the creature the moment it wakes. Rejected by every human it meets, the creature kills Victor's brother William (and frames Justine, who is executed), demands a mate, and, when Victor destroys the half-made female, kills Clerval and then Elizabeth on her wedding night. Victor pursues the creature to the Arctic and dies on Walton's ship; the creature mourns him and vanishes into the dark to die.

passage.quote: I saw the pale student of unhallowed arts kneeling beside the thing he had put together
passage.use: Shelley's 1831 account of the waking vision that became the novel. Note "unhallowed" (unholy) and "thing": before we have read a page, the creator is a student and the creation is not yet a person.

flags: The exact night of the ghost-story proposal and of Mary's waking dream is uncertain: her 1831 account compresses events, and Polidori's diary points to mid-June 1816. Present the 1831 story as her own later recollection.
The extent of Percy Shelley's edits to the 1818 manuscript is debated (Charles E. Robinson's 2008 edition marks his contributions). He wrote the 1818 Preface; the novel is Mary's.
The first-edition print run is usually given as about 500 copies; treat it as approximate.

segments.script: What the book is about (no spoilers): A ship's captain, Robert Walton, sailing toward the North Pole, writes letters to his sister. In the ice he rescues a dying stranger, Victor Frankenstein, who tells him how, as a young student, he discovered the secret of life and built a living being. What happens to Victor, his family and his creation is told in three nested voices: Walton's, Victor's and, at the center, the creature's own. The book asks what we owe the things we make and the people we reject. Themes to track: creation and responsibility: what a maker owes what it makes; watch how often the creature asks to be cared for and how Victor answers. ambition and knowledge: the hunger to discover, shared by Walton and Victor; ask whether the book condemns curiosity or something more specific. isolation and companionship: almost every character is cut off from someone; notice who is allowed to belong and why. nature and nurture: is anyone born a monster, or are monsters made by how they are treated? the sublime: mountains, ice and storms that awe and dwarf human beings.

lessonPlan.title: Frankenstein unit
lessonPlan.author: Mary Shelley
lessonPlan.editionNote: The reading text is Mary Shelley's revised 1831 edition (Standard Ebooks, from Project Gutenberg #42324), which also prints the 1818 Preface and the 1831 Introduction. In 1818 Elizabeth is Victor's cousin; in 1831 she is the orphaned daughter of a Milanese nobleman, adopted by Victor's mother. Chapter breaks also differ (e.g. around Chapter III). Cite this edition.
lessonPlan.gradeBand: Grades 9–12 (also 7–8; scales to graduate via rigor levels)

strategies.label: Wait time
strategies.howTo: Pause at least 3 seconds after asking (5 to 10 for DOK 3 and 4 questions) before calling on anyone, and pause again after a student answers so others can add on. Call on students at random, not only volunteers.

strategies.label: Think-pair-share
strategies.howTo: One minute of silent thinking or jotting, two minutes with a partner, then pairs report. Use it for every DOK 3 and 4 question so all students rehearse an answer.

strategies.label: Follow-up probes
strategies.howTo: Answer a response with a probe instead of a verdict: ask for the line that proves it, ask "why?" or "how do you know?", or ask another student to agree, extend or challenge.

strategies.label: Student-generated questions
strategies.howTo: Students write their own questions at each level (a recall, a "why/how" and a "should/what if" question), trade them, and answer a classmate's. The teacher picks one or two for the whole class.

strategies.label: Turn and talk
strategies.howTo: A 60-second partner check for literal questions, so every student says the answer aloud before one is called on.

strategies.label: Cold call with support
strategies.howTo: Call on a student by name after the wait time; if they are stuck, offer a choice of two answers or let them "phone a friend" and come back to them.

strategies.label: Socratic circle
strategies.howTo: Inner circle discusses for 5 minutes while the outer circle tracks evidence and questions; then swap.

strategies.label: Four corners / take a stand
strategies.howTo: Students move to Agree / Somewhat agree / Somewhat disagree / Disagree and must cite a line to defend the position; anyone may move after hearing evidence.

literal.label: Literal / recall
literal.scaffold: Sentence starter: “In this chapter, … because the text says …”
literal.extension: Note how this detail is set up or echoed elsewhere in Frankenstein.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?

inferential.label: Inferential / analytical
inferential.scaffold: Sentence starter: “The text says …, which suggests … because …”
inferential.extension: Test your reading against one critical approach (formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist) and say what it adds.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

evaluative.label: Evaluative / synthesis / creative
evaluative.scaffold: Sentence starter: “I (dis)agree that … because …; someone might object that …, but …”
evaluative.extension: Situate your judgment in a critical conversation about Frankenstein: whose reading does yours support or challenge?
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the chapter to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

questioning.alignment: Questioning design (our description; see docs/questioning-alignment.md): every lesson offers questions at three cognitive levels with DOK tags, built-in wait time, follow-up probes after each answer, think-pair-share for higher-order items and a student-generated question routine, with a level-specific focus set for each of the eleven rigor levels. It is designed to support classroom observation frameworks such as the NIET Teaching Standards Rubric (Questioning indicator); it is not NIET material and is not endorsed by NIET.

essayAssignments.title: Essay: The costs of unchecked ambition

middleSchool.label: Middle School
middleSchool.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track): write a five-paragraph essay explaining what Frankenstein teaches about the costs of unchecked ambition. Use at least three quotations from passages your teacher selects from different parts of the book.

hsFreshman.label: HS Freshman
hsFreshman.text: Write a multi-paragraph essay explaining how Mary Shelley develops the costs of unchecked ambition in Frankenstein. Use evidence from the beginning, middle and end of the book.

hsSophomore.label: HS Sophomore
hsSophomore.text: Write an argumentative essay analyzing how Mary Shelley develops the costs of unchecked ambition across Frankenstein. Trace the idea through at least three chapters and address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.label: HS Junior
